rows.title: Farm Workers Face Double Threat: Wildfire Smoke And COVID-19
rows.standfirst: Farm workers in California are facing the double health threat of working during the coronavirus pandemic and fire season. Wildfire smoke often makes the air quality dangerous for harvesting produce.

rows.title: The Murderer, The Boy King, And The Invention Of Modern Finance
rows.standfirst: John Law killed a man in a duel, brought the first paper money to France, and became one of the richest people in the world. Then it all collapsed.

rows.title: More Job Growth, But Slower
rows.standfirst: The August unemployment numbers were better than expected. But doesn't mean the labor market is the picture of health.

rows.title: Banning Evictions Should Help The Economy. But Can The CDC Do That?
rows.standfirst: Jerome Powell, the chair of the Federal Reserve, told NPR today that keeping people in their houses and 'connected to the economy' will cost money now, but pay dividends later.

rows.title: Transcript: NPR's Full Interview With Fed Chairman Jerome Powell
rows.standfirst: In an interview on Friday with NPR's Steve Inskeep, Federal Reserve Board Chairman Jerome Powell took questions about the current financial crisis, income inequality and about economic recovery.

rows.title: Fed's Jerome Powell: Jobless Rate Better Than Expected; Recovery To Take A Long Time
rows.standfirst: In an interview with NPR, Powell says it may take years before the economy has fully recovered. He says practicing social distancing and wearing masks is essential for the economy to rebound.

rows.title: President Trump's New COVID-19 Adviser Is Making Public Health Experts Nervous
rows.standfirst: Dr. Scott Atlas is a radiologist from Stanford with some unorthodox ideas about managing the pandemic. The White House says his thinking is just what's needed, but scientists aren't so sure.

rows.title: Job Gains Slowed Again In August As Employers Added 1.4 Million Jobs
rows.standfirst: Fewer jobs were added to the economy last month even as the unemployment rate fell to 8.4%. Job growth has slowed since June in a sign of what could be a long and painful recovery from the recession.

rows.title: Keeping The 'Odd' Family Tool Business Sharp Through 3 Generations
rows.standfirst: A father and son reflect how their family has honed toolmaking through three generations at their Brooklyn, N.Y., shop. Despite pandemic stresses, they hope to be in business well into the future.

rows.title: 'Bad Optics' Or Something More? Moderna Executives' Stock Sales Raise Concerns
rows.standfirst: Moderna is currently developing a promising, yet still unproven, vaccine against the coronavirus. But Moderna executives have already sold tens of millions of dollars worth of stock in the company.

rows.title: They Teach Chinese Kids English Online. Now They're Caught In Trump's War On TikTok
rows.standfirst: ByteDance-owned tutoring app GOGOKID employes about 4,000 American teachers. Trump's crack down on TikTok could mean those instructors will lose their jobs.

rows.title: Overrated Or Underrated: The Nobel Edition
rows.standfirst: Nobel economics prize winners Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee on whether foreign aid, french bread and dating an economist are overrated or underrated.

rows.title: Dow Drops Over 800 Points As Hot Tech Stocks Reverse Course
rows.standfirst: After days of record gains, the stock market suddenly falls to earth, with shares of Apple, Tesla and Facebook leading the way down.

rows.title: Facebook Clamps Down On Posts, Ads That Could Undermine U.S. Presidential Election
rows.standfirst: "We're increasingly seeing attempts to undermine the legitimacy of our elections from within our own borders," Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg says.

rows.title: New Jobless Claims Drop Below 1 Million, But There's A Caveat
rows.standfirst: Another 881,000 people applied for state unemployment benefits last week, the Labor Department says. That's down from the previous week, but the report comes with an asterisk.

rows.title: The Birth Of The Greenback
rows.standfirst: In the mid-1800s, the US had 8,370 kinds of money. How that happened, and what it meant for the US economy.

rows.title: 'We Had To Take Action': States In Mexico Move To Ban Junk Food Sales To Minors
rows.standfirst: "The damage of this kind of diet is even more visible because of the pandemic," says a Oaxaca legislator who spearheaded a law against the sale of junk food and soda to minors. The idea is spreading.

rows.title: Long Before Cambridge Analytica And Facebook, Simulmatics Linked Data And Politics
rows.standfirst: In If Then , author and New Yorker writer Jill Lepore unearths Simulmatics' story and makes the argument that the company paved the way for our 21st-century obsession with data and prediction.

rows.title: Oracle's Deal For TikTok May Not Include A Purchase
rows.standfirst: Oracle says it's ready to be a "trusted technology provider" for the hit video-sharing app. A bid for TikTok's U.S. operations by tech giant Microsoft has been rejected.

rows.title: As Auto Industry Roars Back, Worker Shortages Throw Up Roadblocks
rows.standfirst: The U.S. auto industry has an absenteeism problem. The word might bring to mind people playing hooky, but during a pandemic there are lots of good reasons people might not show up to work.

rows.title: Despite A New Federal Ban, Many Renters Are Still Getting Evicted
rows.standfirst: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ordered a nationwide eviction ban for people who can't pay rent and have no place to go. It's helping some, but many others are getting evicted anyway.

rows.title: AstraZeneca Resumes Its COVID-19 Vaccine Trials In The U.K.
rows.standfirst: The company had placed its worldwide vaccine trials on hold for several days. It now says a safety review by regulators and reviewers is complete. No word on when studies in the U.S. might resume.

rows.title: Waste Land
rows.standfirst: Recycling plastic has never worked very well. So who convinced us this was a good idea? In this episode, we might have the answer. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: The Science of Hoops
rows.standfirst: The three-point shot has revolutionized basketball, but its unintended consequences could mean trouble for the sport's future.

rows.title: More Groceries, Less Gas: The Pandemic Is Shaking Up The Cost Of Living
rows.standfirst: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in August and 1.3% over the last 12 months. Some economists say that official measure understates inflation, because the pandemic has changed both what and how we buy.

rows.title: A Mining Company Blew Up A 46,000-Year-Old Aboriginal Site. Its CEO Is Resigning
rows.standfirst: In May, mining giant Rio Tinto blasted through two ancient rock shelters in Western Australia in order to mine iron ore. The company has been under rising pressure to hold executives accountable.

rows.title: Fortnite Fight: CEO Explains Why He Launched War Against Apple, Google
rows.standfirst: The Epic Games CEO tells NPR that the tech titans are abusing their power and exploiting developers by demanding a 30% cut of every app purchase made on a smartphone or tablet.

rows.title: Making The Most Of Scarce Space
rows.standfirst: Lockdowns, working from home, and remote learning have all made personal domestic space more scarce. Emily Anthes has some solutions.

rows.title: 57 People Face Federal Charges Of Defrauding Coronavirus Relief Program
rows.standfirst: Prosecutors say those charged attempted to steal more than $175 million from the Paycheck Protection Program, which is meant to provide relief to small businesses impacted by the pandemic.

rows.title: Twitter's New Rules Aim To Prevent Confusion Around The 2020 Vote
rows.standfirst: Twitter will label or remove posts that spread misinformation. Social media companies are under pressure to curb the spread of false claims and prevent interference from foreign and domestic actors.

rows.title: Jamaican Monetary Policy: Behind The Music
rows.standfirst: Jamaica's Central Bank has a unique way of explaining its policies: Reggae music videos. The Indicator talks with the Central Bank about why they've taken this unique approach.

rows.title: Shop For A Pair Of Shoes To Go With That Bread. Grocery Chain, DSW Team Up
rows.standfirst: The Midwestern chain Hy-Vee says DSW shoe outlets are opening in six of its supermarkets in Minnesota. Grocery shoppers will be able to try on shoes, then order online.

rows.title: Microsoft To Buy Bethesda In $7.5 Billion Deal, Acquiring Fallout, The Elder Scrolls
rows.standfirst: The deal is set to be one of the largest ever acquisitions in the video game industry. Once the deal is finalized, Microsoft will own popular franchises such as Wolfenstein, Quake, and DOOM.

rows.title: Founder Of Zero-Emissions Truck Startup Resigns After Fraud Allegations
rows.standfirst: Trevor Milton's startup Nikola is working on hydrogen-powered big rigs. Milton has been accused of making misleading claims about the company's technology, which he has denied.

rows.title: Stocks Tumble On Big Banks' Role In Money Laundering Report, Fears Of Relief Delay
rows.standfirst: The Dow falls more than 500 points as a report says large global banks were involved in transactions flagged as possible money laundering and hopes dim for Congress to pass another relief measure.

rows.title: Trump's TikTok Deal: What Just Happened And Why Does It Matter?
rows.standfirst: President Trump is claiming victory after blessing a deal in which Oracle and Walmart will own a stake of TikTok, but experts wonder whether the terms of the agreement will really change anything.

rows.title: Voice Of America CEO In The Hot Seat: Democratic Lawmakers Bear Down On Pack
rows.standfirst: Two senior Democratic lawmakers are sharply questioning moves by Trump appointee Michael Pack, the CEO of the U.S. Agency for Global Media. The agency oversees the Voice of America.

rows.title: 'Hard, Dirty Job': Cities Struggle To Clear Garbage Glut In Stay-At-Home World
rows.standfirst: As people stay at home, they are putting out more trash, from pizza boxes to cardboard delivery boxes. That's putting a big strain on residential garbage collectors.

rows.title: Federal Judge Blocks Trump Administration's U.S. WeChat Ban
rows.standfirst: A judge in San Francisco said Trump's order targeting the popular Chinese-owned app has a "modest" basis in national security and represents a free speech violation for U.S. users of the app.

rows.title: TikTok Ban Averted: Trump Gives Oracle-Walmart Deal His 'Blessing'
rows.standfirst: U.S. tech company Oracle is joining hands with Walmart to become a technology partner with TikTok, an arrangement that satisfies the White House's concerns over the security of American user data.

rows.title: Nation's Largest Business Lobby Backs Vulnerable Democrats For Reelection
rows.standfirst: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has endorsed 30 House Democrats for reelection, the highest number of Democrats to earn the business lobby's support in at least a decade.

rows.title: Apple v Everybody
rows.standfirst: When Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney sued Apple over its App Store, it started a war about antitrust and the internet.

rows.title: Downturn Start-Ups: A Conversation With Guy Raz
rows.standfirst: Since the pandemic started, nearly 100,000 businesses have closed permanently. Opening a business now might seem crazy. But downturn start-ups have some advantages.

rows.title: Movie Industry Adapts, Plus LeVar Burton Reads
rows.standfirst: The movie industry is hurting. Most theaters in the U.S. are still shut down, and who knows when—or if—audiences will pack into theaters again. Adam B. Vary and Angelique Jackson of Variety talk about the state of the movie industry and how it's adapted, for better or worse, in this pandemic. Also, Sam talks to actor LeVar Burton about reading, why we like being read to, what he really wanted you to learn from Reading Rainbow , and the latest season of his podcast LeVar Burton Reads .

rows.title: U.S. To Bar Downloads Of TikTok, WeChat
rows.standfirst: As of Sunday, no mobile app store in the U.S. will be allowed to distribute or maintain the popular Chinese-owned apps, the Commerce Department says.

rows.title: Trump's Tiny Taxes
rows.standfirst: A totally refreshing 20 minutes or so of infotainment related to Trump, taxes and toy wooden arrows. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: 'I Like What I See': FAA Chief Flies 737 Max, But Not Ready To Recertify Plane
rows.standfirst: Steve Dickson took a Boeing 737 Max on a test flight Wednesday and says "It responded well," as regulators inch closer to ungrounding the troubled jetliner.

rows.title: Big Donors & Pay-To-Play Politics
rows.standfirst: The Center for Public Integrity joins The Indicator with an excerpt from The Heist, a new podcast exploring money and politics in the Trump Administration.

rows.title: Juggling Financial Stress And Caregiving, Parents Are 'Very Not OK' In The Pandemic
rows.standfirst: The pandemic economy is squeezing families with kids: 74% of those earning less than $100,000 report serious financial woes, in an NPR poll. Experts worry about lasting impacts on kids' mental health.

rows.title: The Indicator World Tour
rows.standfirst: The Indicator brings listeners economic indicators from the other six continents.

rows.title: Disney Lays Off 28,000 Workers, 67% Are Part-Time Employees
rows.standfirst: The Walt Disney Company's theme parks, resorts and cruises have been devastated by COVID-19. Disney announced it is laying off the workers from its Parks, Experiences and Products division.

rows.title: Anita Hill On Sexual Harassment In Hollywood And Beyond
rows.standfirst: Anita Hill, chair of the Hollywood Commission, discusses a new report's findings on sexual harassment in the industry. She also discusses Brett Kavanaugh's confirmation battle and Joe Biden.

rows.title: You Literally Can't Believe The Facts Tucker Carlson Tells You. So Say Fox's Lawyers
rows.standfirst: Fox News viewers don't expect facts from Tucker Carlson, according to network lawyers who defended their star in a slander lawsuit filed by a woman who said she had an affair with President Trump.

rows.title: How Operation Warp Speed's Big Vaccine Contracts Could Stay Secret
rows.standfirst: More than $6 billion in federal funding has been routed through a firm that manages defense contracts, making the agreements subject to less federal scrutiny and transparency.

rows.title: 'Russia Doesn't Have To Make Fake News': Biggest Election Threat Is Closer To Home
rows.standfirst: National security officials say Russia is again trying to disrupt the election. But this time, it doesn't have to work so hard because Americans are spreading mistruths and doubts about the election.

rows.title: 'This Is Too Much': Working Moms Are Reaching The Breaking Point During The Pandemic
rows.standfirst: The coronavirus did not create the struggles that working mothers face daily. But it has exacerbated them and made them more visible, forcing women of all income levels to make hard choices.

rows.title: How A Beloved Gemstone Became A Symbol Of Environmental Tragedy In Myanmar
rows.standfirst: Decades of mining for jade has left the landscape desolate. Local activists want to make a change — but can they stand up to the powerful companies that dominate the industry?

rows.title: Most People Can't Afford Legal Help. 1 Reformer Wants To Change That
rows.standfirst: Bar fight!

rows.title: Legal Fight Over Trump's Financial Records Grinds On Even As Tax Details Spill Out
rows.standfirst: The president is waging multiple court battles to shield his finances from scrutiny, including two cases involving subpoenas issued to his personal accounting firm.

rows.title: Pandemic Threatens Long-Term Job Security After Hospitality Industry Layoffs
rows.standfirst: Experts say the hotel industry may not return to pre-pandemic levels until 2023. Hospitality workers are bearing the brunt of this long downturn.
